p.x:
My grandma has a beautiful garden. There is green grass in the middle and many flowers around it. Her favourite flower is the rose. She has red, pink and white ones.
She also has tall sunflowers next to the wall. They are taller than me! At the back, she grows tomatoes and carrots. Every summer, we eat them for dinner.
On her balcony, Grandma has small plants in a pot. When a leaf turns yellow, she cuts it off. I love helping her in the garden at weekends.

Gardening is one of the world's most popular hobbies, and you don't need a big space to start. Many people in cities grow a herb such as basil or mint on a balcony, or keep a houseplant indoors.
To begin, you need a few simple tools: a spade for digging, gloves to protect your hands, and a watering can or a hose. If you have a lawn, you will also need to mow it regularly. In autumn, people rake the fallen leaves and carry them away in a wheelbarrow.
Plants need sunlight, water and good soil. Seeds grow into small seedlings, and their roots spread underground. Worms help by making the soil healthy. When fruit is ripe, it's ready to pick. In hot weather, plants can wilt quickly if you forget to water them.
Gardening also brings challenges. Snails, insects and other pests can eat your plants, and roses have sharp thorns. Many gardeners prune their bushes and hedges to keep them neat. But the reward comes when flowers bloom and their colourful petals fill the garden. Many people say gardening makes them feel calm and happy.

As cities grow and green space disappears, people are finding creative ways to garden. In Bangkok and Singapore, a rooftop garden can turn an empty concrete space into a source of vegetables and a refuge for birds and insects. In Britain, there is a long tradition of renting an allotment, a small piece of public land where residents grow fruit and vegetables; waiting lists in some cities are now several years long.
Technology is also changing the way food is grown. Hydroponics allows plants to grow in nutrient-rich water rather than soil, using far less space and water than traditional farming. Indoor farms stacked with shelves of lettuce can now be found in warehouses in the middle of cities.
At the same time, many gardeners are returning to traditional, natural methods. Instead of chemicals, they use manure and compost to enrich the soil, and spread mulch around plants to keep moisture in and weeds out. They choose flowers that attract bees and butterflies, which pollinate crops and are essential for food production. Planting perennials, which return year after year, reduces the need for constant replanting.
For beginners, even small successes are rewarding: watching a seed germinate, or growing a new plant from a cutting taken from a friend's garden. Those who seem to grow anything effortlessly are said to have green fingers. Yet even the least experienced gardener can usually keep a succulent alive, since these plants store water in their thick leaves.
